strengths: The proposed combination of covariance whitening, coordinate screening, and LDA addresses a relevant problem with an identifiable audience in high-dimensional statistics and machine learning. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b10/review-experiment-4y15ycc1/call-e36213819d04417cafce9733c81f9741/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
Using entrywise eigenvector perturbation bounds is a promising analytical strategy for studying classification with dense covariance matrices and strong latent factors.
The experiments include relevant competing methods, 200 Monte Carlo replications with standard deviations, and two real datasets. The reported random-covariance and real-data results are encouraging.
The motivating example, explicit algorithms, and discussion distinguishing sparsity in whitened coordinates from sparsity in the discriminant direction help communicate the main idea.
weaknesses: Required: The central theoretical guarantees are not established under the stated spike assumptions. Condition 3 only requires λ_k = O(p), which supplies no lower bound or sufficient eigengap. Nevertheless, the proofs use comparable spike magnitudes and bounds requiring strong spikes; the comparison immediately preceding Eq. (B.15), for example, does not follow from Condition 3. Taking λ_1 = p and λ_d = 1 is permitted. The necessary lower bounds and restrictions on d must be stated, and the dependent results checked under those assumptions.

Required: The convergence conditions do not match the proofs. Theorem 3 inherits log p = o(n), but Appendix B.4 concludes using the stronger condition (log n)(log p) = o(n). Theorem 5 allows log p = O(n), under which neither the estimation bound nor the screening threshold necessarily vanishes; exact support recovery is therefore unsupported without additional signal restrictions. Supply arguments establishing the stated results or narrow the theorem statements and headline claims.

Required: Section 5.1 incorrectly treats Fisher's Gaussian LDA rule as Bayes optimal for general elliptical distributions with unequal class priors. For a common radial density generator h, the Bayes comparison involves log h(q_2) − log h(q_1) plus the log prior ratio, where q_i is the squared Mahalanobis distance to class i. This generally produces a different boundary. Sub-Gaussian tails do not resolve this issue. Restrict the extension to appropriate cases, such as equal priors with a common decreasing generator, or derive the appropriate classifier.

Required: The reported oracle errors conflict materially with the specified simulation models. For Model 2, the stated means and covariance give squared Mahalanobis separation [10 − 100ρ/(1 + 19ρ)]/(1 − ρ). At ρ = 0.9, the resulting Bayes error is approximately 0.0196%, whereas Table 5 reports 5.40%. For Model 1 at ρ = 0.8, the theoretical error is approximately 0.0221%, whereas Table 2 reports 0.19%. These discrepancies are far larger than plausible Monte Carlo variation. Audit the simulations and tables or correct the model descriptions before relying on these comparisons.

Required: Resolve discrepancies between the defined estimator, its tuning, and the theory. Section 2.3 defines Λ̂ as the leading eigenvalues of the sample covariance, which already include the noise contribution, but then adds σ̂² again when constructing D̂. Clarify and consistently implement the eigenvalue parameterization. The same section promises consistent estimation of d, yet no corresponding result is supplied. The experimental 90% explained-variance rule does not generally recover the true spike count: in Model 1 with ρ = 0.5, the single population spike accounts for only about half the total variance. Either justify the selected tuning procedure or delimit the guarantees to the procedure actually analyzed.

Necessary clarification: The reported feature counts measure selected whitened coordinates, whose computation generally requires all original variables because the whitening matrix is dense. Tables describing these counts as model size should make this distinction explicit. Claims of uniformly highest accuracy or smallest feature count also exceed the tables: for example, Table 2 at ρ = 0.9 reports 0.22% error for PCLDA versus approximately 0% for several competitors. Competitive performance remains a potentially useful finding, but the comparisons need accurate qualification.

Optional: After resolving the correctness issues, experiments varying sample size, dimension, spike strength, and approximate sparsity would help readers understand when the method works well. Sensitivity analysis for the explained-variance threshold would also strengthen practical guidance.
